1→# Architecture
   2→
   3→This document explains the system to someone who has read the README and has five minutes.
   4→Every claim here describes the code as it stands; nothing is planned or partial except where
   5→the Limits section says so plainly.
   6→
   7→## Overview
   8→
   9→Ryde is a multi-agent dispute resolution system for ride-hailing: a party files a dispute
  10→through a web intake form, and the system resolves the two categories it handles — route
  11→deviation and no-show charge — end to end. Three agents do the work: a Rider Advocate and a
  12→Driver Advocate each build their side's case from the evidence, and a Judge weighs both
  13→cases, applies company policy and issues a ruling with a confidence score. Every computed
  14→figure the agents argue from comes from a deterministic Evidence Pack calculated in Python
  15→before any model is called; agents cite pack fields by reference and are forbidden from
  16→doing their own arithmetic, and the only other number they see is the amount the party
  17→asked for. The decisions that must never depend on a model's obedience — the confidence
  18→threshold, the SGD 50 autonomous cap, the requirement that a route ruling rest on a measured
  19→deviation, the one-round follow-up limit, and the routing of out-of-scope categories to
  20→human review — are enforced in Python code, not asked of the model in a prompt. The system
  21→has two surfaces: an operator console that shows the full case file and the agent-to-agent
  22→traffic, and a party page where the filing party submits the form and reads only what they
  23→are allowed to read.
  24→
  25→## Diagram
  26→
  27→The whole system on one page. A dispute arrives either through the web intake form or the
  28→command-line runner; the two swappable inputs (the policy document and the dataset pack)
  29→enter from the side. Every step of a run lands in the event log, and the operator console
  30→renders the event strip embedded in the case file — opening each event's full payload from
  31→the run files the operator attaches.
  32→
  33→```mermaid
  34→flowchart TD
  35→    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> B["Server"]
  36→    PACK --> CL["Command-line runner"]
  37→    A["Rider intake form"] --> B
  38→    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
  39→    CL --> C
  40→    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
  41→    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
  42→    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
  43→    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
  44→    POL --> J["Judge"]
  45→    E --> RA
  46→    E --> DA
  47→    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
  48→    DA --> S
  49→    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
  50→    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
  51→    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
  52→    S -- "No" --> J
  53→    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
  54→    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
  55→    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
  56→    O2 -- "Candidate ruling queued" --> H
  57→    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
  58→    J -.-> L
  59→    L -- "Embedded in the case file" --> K["Operator console"]
  60→```
  61→
  62→## Components
  63→
  64→| Component | File(s) | Responsibility |
  65→|---|---|---|
  66→| Pipeline | `app/pipeline.py` | Runs one dispute end to end, moves the case between agents, records every step |
  67→| Dispute record and routing | `app/dispute.py` | Parses the two record shapes, normalises categories, routes out-of-scope filings away |
  68→| Evidence layer | `app/evidence/compute.py` | Computes the Evidence Pack by plain arithmetic; a missing input inside a record becomes a null with a note, never a guess — but a route case with no trip record, or a no-show case with no cancellation record, aborts the run before any pack is built |
  69→| Agent scaffolding | `app/agents/base.py` | Shared prompts, the LLM call, and citation validation against the pack and the policy |
  70→| Rider Advocate | `app/agents/rider_advocate.py` | Argues the rider's side from the pack and the policy |
  71→| Driver Advocate | `app/agents/driver_advocate.py` | Argues the driver's side from the pack and the policy |
  72→| Judge | `app/agents/judge.py` | Weighs both cases, issues one ruling, withholds it behind the gates |
  73→| Event log | `app/events.py` | The append-only record of who said what to whom, with full payloads on disk |
  74→| Output contracts | `app/schemas.py` | The typed shapes agents must produce; builds the party-facing decision message |
  75→| Policy loader | `app/policy.py` | Reads the policy document, extracts rule IDs, fails loudly when it is missing |
  76→| Mock LLM | `app/llm/mock.py` | Deterministic stand-in provider; its free-text fields — claim summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation — carry a `MOCK` prefix, while actions, rule IDs and evidence refs do not |
  77→| Tencent adapter | `app/llm/tencent.py` | The real provider: calls one Tencent Cloud ADP app per agent over HTTP |
  78→| HTTP server | `app/server.py` | The intake API, the party view allowlist, and static files for both pages |
  79→| Command-line runner | `app/cli.py` | Runs one dispute from the terminal and prints the event strip |
  80→| Runtime configuration | `app/config.json` | Confidence threshold, autonomous cap, default dataset pack, provider settings |
  81→| Operator console | `ui/app.js` | Renders the case file: grievance, evidence, both claims, resolution, event strip |
  82→| Party page | `ui/party/party.js` | The intake form and the outcome view the filing party sees |
  83→| Policy document | `docs/policy.md` | The rule set the agents cite, with per-rule provenance |
  84→
  85→## Lifecycle of a dispute
  86→
  87→`run_dispute` in `app/pipeline.py` walks one dispute through these steps, in this order,
  88→emitting an event at each:
  89→
  90→1. `run.started` — the system records the dispute id, category, LLM provider, confidence
  91→   threshold and the policy rule IDs in force.
  92→2. `dispute.filed` — the raw intake-form submission is logged exactly as it arrived.
  93→3. **Routing.** If the category is outside the two handled ones, the run emits
  94→   `dispute.routed_to_human_review`, then `party.notified` with the neutral support message,
  95→   then `run.completed` — and no agent runs at all.
  96→4. `evidence.pack_built` — the Evidence Pack is computed in Python, before any LLM call,
  97→   and offered to the agents as the source of every computed figure — the only other
  98→   number they see is the amount the party claimed.
  99→5. `case.assigned` — once to each advocate.
 100→6. Each advocate runs and emits `advocate.case_submitted` to the Judge with its case. When
 101→   an advocate needs more from the filing party, it selects offered slot IDs and emits
 102→   `advocate.follow_up_requested` in the first round with both the selected slots and the
 103→   rendered questions. Code renders a bank sentence for a rider-filed dispute, or a form
 104→   sentence from an intake label for either filer; any question text written by the model
 105→   is ignored. The party-safety check remains a backstop, and only rendered questions that
 106→   pass it reach the party.
 107→7. **Stop and ask.** If there are questions to send and the dispute does not already carry
 108→   the party's answers, the run stops before the Judge: `party.notified` carries the
 109→   rendered questions — or, when none survive the backstop, plain template questions the
 110→   pipeline builds for blank intake fields — then `run.completed` records the `needs_info`
 111→   outcome. The party's answers start a fresh run, which is guaranteed to reach the Judge.
 112→8. `judge.deliberation_started` — both cases are handed to the Judge together.
 113→9. The Judge rules: `judge.ruling_issued` when every gate passes, or
 114→   `judge.ruling_withheld` when one fails — the candidate ruling is recorded either way.
 115→10. `party.notified` — the message the parties actually receive, as opposed to what was
 116→    decided internally.
 117→11. `run.completed` — the outcome is recorded and the case file is written.
 118→
 119→## The four outcomes
 120→
 121→| Outcome | When it happens | Did the Judge run? | Party page shows |
 122→|---|---|---|---|
 123→| `ruled` | The Judge issued a ruling and every gate passed | Yes | `decided` |
 124→| `withheld` | A gate stopped the ruling: confidence below threshold, amount above the cap, or an unmeasured deviation on a route case | Yes — the candidate is recorded for a human reviewer, never delivered | `under_review` |
 125→| `human_review` | The category is outside the two the agents handle | No — routed away before any agent | `passed_to_support` |
 126→| `needs_info` | The advocates selected offered follow-up slots in the first round, or a blank form answer produced a template question | No — the run stops before the Judge | `needs_info` |
 127→
 128→## Gates enforced in code
 129→
 130→Six gates stand between a filing and a ruling, and each is enforced in Python, not asked of
 131→the model in a prompt:
 132→
 133→| Gate | File | Condition as written in code |
 134→|---|---|---|
 135→| Confidence threshold | `app/agents/judge.py` | `ruling.confidence < confidence_threshold` — the threshold is 0.65, read from `app/config.json` |
 136→| ESC-4, the autonomous cap | `app/agents/judge.py` | A money ruling whose `recommended_amount_sgd` exceeds the cap is withheld; the cap is SGD 50 from `app/config.json` |
 137→| ESC-2, unmeasured deviation | `app/agents/judge.py` | On a route-deviation case, `pack.route.deviation_pct is null` withholds the ruling — a route ruling must name the deviation it rests on |
 138→| One-round follow-up limit | `app/pipeline.py` | `if questions and not dispute.follow_up_answers` — a dispute is asked at most once; with answers present the Judge always runs and fresh questions are recorded but not sent |
 139→| Out-of-scope routing | `app/pipeline.py` | `if not dispute.is_agent_handled` — anything outside route deviation and no-show charge goes to human review before any agent runs; an unrecognised category normalises to "other" in `app/dispute.py` |
 140→| Answer once | `app/server.py` | The answers route claims the run with an exclusive create (`O_CREAT \| O_EXCL`) before re-running it — a `needs_info` run can be answered exactly once and cannot produce two rulings |
 141→
 142→Why in code? Because a prompt is a request — a model can misread it, and there is no
 143→recourse when it does. Code is a guarantee: the branch either runs or it does not, and the
 144→event log shows which. ESC-4 in particular moves money, so it must not depend on the LLM
 145→having read its instructions carefully.
 146→
 147→## Observability
 148→
 149→Every run writes three things under `runs/<run_id>/`:
 150→
 151→- `events.jsonl` — one JSON line per event, append-only, never rewritten: who sent what to
 152→  whom, when, with a one-line summary.
 153→- `payloads/` — the full payload behind each event, named by sequence number and event
 154→  type, so the strip stays readable and the detail stays one click away.
 155→- `case_file.json` — the assembled record: what was claimed, the evidence pack, both
 156→  advocate cases, the resolution, and the event strip. Self-contained, so one file tells
 157→  the whole story of one run.
 158→
 159→A run filed through the server writes one more file: `dispute.json`, the record the pipeline
 160→actually ran on (the command-line runner does not write it). When a `needs_info` run is
 161→answered, its directory also gains `answered.json`, recording which run the answers
 162→produced.
 163→
 164→The operator console (`ui/app.js`) renders the case file: the event strip shows one row per
 165→event — sequence, time, sender to recipient, summary — and expanding a row opens the full
 166→payload from the run directory attached in the browser. Payload references are sanitised, so
 167→a console loaded with a hostile file can be pointed at nothing outside the run. The
 168→command-line runner prints the same strip to the terminal.
 169→
 170→## What the parties see
 171→
 172→`party_view` in `app/server.py` is an allowlist that fails closed. The party page is handed
 173→exactly five keys — run id, dispute id, status, message, questions — and any malformed case
 174→file degrades to the neutral under-review message with no questions. A withheld ruling's
 175→amount and the Judge's confidence are structurally absent from everything the party is
 176→sent, not merely unrendered. `party_message_for_ruling` in `app/schemas.py` composes the
 177→decision message in code from structured fields — the action, the amount, and the plain
 178→titles of the policy rules cited — and the Judge's explanation never crosses this boundary:
 179→it stays in the operator console. Every non-decision status shows a canonical constant
 180→message, whatever a stale or planted case file might say. The two kinds of party-facing text
 181→are protected differently. The decision message is composed in code from structured fields,
 182→so nothing model-written reaches it: it names the action and the amount — a no-action ruling
 183→carries no amount — and at most three rule titles, never the escalation (ESC) rules. On a
 184→decided view the message leads with a demo notice whenever the ruling's LLM record does not
 185→prove the real provider — only a record that is a non-array dict whose provider field is
 186→exactly `tencent` suppresses it, and any other record, missing, mock or malformed, keeps it —
 187→so a decision made on an illustrative run never reads like a live review, while a proven
 188→real-provider decision shows no notice.
 189→Follow-up questions are selected by the advocates as slot IDs; code renders each sentence
 190→from the fixed category bank or from an intake form label. Bank slots are offered only when
 191→the rider filed, while form slots work for either filer. Any question text written by the
 192→model is ignored, so no model-written text reaches a party. The word check (`is_party_safe`,
 193→applied in `_questions_for_party` in `app/pipeline.py` and again in `party_view`) remains a
 194→backstop, as it is for the code-composed decision message. When no rendered question survives,
 195→the pipeline falls back to plain template questions built from the form's own labels. A run
 196→that asked for more information is answered through `POST /api/disputes/<run_id>/answers`, and
 197→the answers start a fresh run on the same dispute.
 198→
 199→## Policy and dataset packs
 200→
 201→`docs/policy.md` is data, not code: rules with IDs (GEN, EV, RD, NS, ESC families),
 202→preconditions written against pack fields in plain language, and per-rule provenance
 203→stating whether a rule comes from Ryde's own published policy, a comparable operator, or
 204→the project team. The pipeline reads it at the path in `app/config.json`; a different
 205→policy document drops in with no code change. Nothing in the code evaluates the
 206→preconditions — the Judge reads the rules and applies them in its reasoning. Citing a rule
 207→that does not exist is recorded rather than blocked: an unknown ID is logged under the
 208→ruling's `validation.unknown_rule_ids` with a note and the ruling still issues, but only
 209→titles of rules the policy actually defines can reach the party message.
 210→
 211→Two dataset packs live under `data/packs/`: `organiser-style-v1` — the default in
 212→`app/config.json` — which holds the corpus in the organisers' record shape, including their
 213→own DISP-002 verbatim; and `ryde-synth-v1`, the same 17 cases in this project's own record
 214→shape. Swapping corpora is a directory copy, never a code change. Each pack carries a
 215→`ground-truth.json` of expected outcomes, kept out of what the agents see: the agents get
 216→the dispute record, the evidence pack and the policy — never the answer — so replayed-run
 217→consistency can be measured honestly.
 218→
 219→## LLM provider
 220→
 221→Agent logic never talks to a vendor SDK. Every agent builds a request and calls one seam:
 222→the `LLMClient` interface in `app/llm/`, a single `complete` method whose response carries
 223→the text plus provenance (provider, model, usage, finish reason). Two adapters implement
 224→it. The mock provider, `app/llm/mock.py`, returns deterministic contract-shaped responses,
 225→so the full pipeline runs with no API key and the same dispute always produces the same
 226→decisions and the same computed figures (the run id and the event timestamps differ from
 227→run to run). Its free-text fields — claim summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation —
 228→carry a `MOCK` prefix, so a mock run can never be mistaken for a real ruling; actions, rule
 229→IDs and evidence refs are not prefixed. The party decision message, composed in code, is
 230→marked differently: on a decided party view it leads with a fixed demo notice stating that
 231→the decision came from an illustrative run and is not a live review, shown whenever the
 232→ruling's LLM record does not prove the Tencent provider, and only a record whose provider
 233→field is exactly `tencent` shows a decision with no notice. The Tencent adapter,
 234→`app/llm/tencent.py`, implements the same interface over Tencent Cloud ADP (Agent
 235→Development Platform). Each agent is its own published ADP app with its own key: Rider
 236→Advocate, Driver Advocate and Judge. The apps carry only a short role card; the adapter
 237→sends the full role prompt on every call, so the prompts live in this repo and every gate
 238→stays in Python. Three things about the endpoint shape the adapter. Tencent's web firewall
 239→blocks prompts that mix backticks with ASCII brackets, so the adapter drops backticks and
 240→sends full-width brackets, which the model reads the same way; a blocked call raises an
 241→error and is never retried. ADP reports errors inside a successful HTTP response, so the
 242→adapter reads every event rather than trusting the status code. The free plan allows 10
 243→calls a minute, so calls are spaced at least 6.5 seconds apart. Any failure raises an
 244→error, and there is no silent fallback to the mock. The mock stays the default provider,
 245→so the tests and a fresh checkout need no keys; `--llm tencent` selects the real model.
 246→
 247→## Limits
 248→
 249→What the system does not do yet, stated plainly:
 250→
 251→- **A failed model call is an error, not a referral.** If a live call fails (the firewall,
 252→  the rate limit, an ADP error or a reply that breaks the output contract), the run stops
 253→  and the party sees a generic error. It is not yet routed to a human reviewer.
 254→- **Amounts must come back as JSON numbers.** A model reply carrying an amount as a string
 255→  is rejected, never converted, because the value moves money.
 256→- **Two categories only.** Route deviation and no-show charge. Property damage and safety
 257→  incidents route to human review by design.
 258→- **The driver-side form is not built.** The party page files as the rider only; the
 259→  pipeline itself accepts driver-filed disputes, but no web form offers it yet.
 260→- **Follow-up wording is code-owned.** Advocates select slot IDs; code renders each question
 261→  from the fixed category bank or an intake form label, and model-written question text is
 262→  ignored. Bank slots are rider-only; form slots are available to either filer.
 263→- **The word check is a backstop.** Rendered follow-up questions and the code-composed decision
 264→  message pass the keyword gate, which is not a semantic guarantee; blank fields still use
 265→  template questions built from the form's own labels.
 266→- **Policy preconditions are not evaluated by code.** The rules are written against pack
 267→  fields in plain language; nothing checks them mechanically, and the Judge applies them by
 268→  reading them.
 269→

1→# Dataset — labelled dispute corpus
   2→
   3→**Version 1.1 · two packs · 17 synthesised cases + the organisers' sample · generated 2026-09-21,
   4→organiser twins 2026-09-23 · policy version 1.0**
   5→
   6→The corpus the system is evaluated against. Like the policy, it is **data, not code**: the
   7→pipeline reads dispute records from a **dataset pack** under `data/packs/`, and a real dataset
   8→drops in with no code change.
   9→
  10→A pack is a directory with `disputes/` (one JSON file per case, named `<dispute_id>.json`),
  11→`ground-truth.json` (the labels) and `pack.json` (the manifest). `app/config.json` names the
  12→default pack; `--pack <name>` selects another for one CLI run.
  13→
  14→```
  15→data/packs/
  16→├── ryde-synth-v1/        our 17 synthesised cases, our record shape
  17→└── organiser-style-v1/   the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers' shape,
  18→                          plus the organisers' own DISP-002, verbatim
  19→```
  20→
  21→---
  22→
  23→## PROVENANCE — read this first
  24→
  25→**Every synthesised case in this corpus was authored by the project team. The one case that was
  26→not — the organisers' sample `DISP-002` — is reproduced byte-for-byte from the file they shared,
  27→and its provenance is theirs, not ours. No real trip, rider, driver, GPS trace or payment appears
  28→anywhere in either pack.**
  29→
  30→The challenge statement promised a sample dataset; one sample dispute (`DISP-002`) arrived on
  31→2026-09-23, which is a sample rather than a corpus, and Ryde publishes no dispute statistics —
  32→confirmed against LTA's Point-to-Point Quality of Service releases (which measure safety, not fare
  33→disputes), CASE's annual complaint reports (which have no ride-hailing category), and Ryde Group's
  34→own SEC filings. The absence is documented, not assumed.
  35→
  36→So the corpus is built rather than collected. Its **shapes** are grounded: the dispute patterns
  37→are modelled on publicly reported Singapore ride-hailing disputes (a driver marking arrival from
  38→the wrong location and letting the clock run; a fare adjusted after a destination change; a mass
  39→ERP mis-rating corrected on the regulator's direction), and the fee amounts and thresholds come
  40→from Ryde's published policy. The **data** is fabricated.
  41→
  42→**What this means for any number measured against it.** An accuracy figure from this corpus
  43→measures whether the system applies *our* policy to *our* cases consistently. It is a measure of
  44→internal consistency and calibration. It is **not** evidence of real-world accuracy, and must
  45→never be presented as one.
  46→
  47→---
  48→
  49→## The two packs
  50→
  51→**`ryde-synth-v1`** is the corpus described below: 17 synthesised cases in our own record shape,
  52→which is documented at the top of `app/dispute.py`.
  53→
  54→**`organiser-style-v1`** is the same 17 cases re-expressed in the shape of the organisers' sample
  55→(`dispute_ticket` / `trip_data` / `gps_telemetry` / `chat_logs` / `app_events`), plus `DISP-002`,
  56→the organisers' own no-show case, copied byte-for-byte from the file they shared and labelled from
  57→their stated ruling. Every synthetic case is a **twin** of its `ryde-synth-v1` counterpart: same
  58→facts, same numbers, different field names. `tests/test_organiser_pack.py` compares the two packs
  59→field by field, and `tests/test_organiser_reader.py` requires the Evidence Pack computed from a
  60→case and from its twin to agree on every number a ruling can rest on — a reader that maps one
  61→field wrong shows up there as a named mismatched field, not as a wrong ruling much later.
  62→
  63→Where the organisers' shape has no slot for something we carry (the claim amount, the intake-form
  64→answers, route-deviation trip fields), the case keeps it in a `ryde_extensions` block; `pack.json`
  65→lists exactly which fields those are. The reader maps the block back, so neither the Evidence Pack
  66→nor the agents need to know which pack a case came from.
  67→
  68→Each synthetic case also carries a top-level `cancellation_policy` stating the terms that govern
  69→it — Ryde's published 3-minute terms for our cases, the organisers' own 5 / 8 minute terms on
  70→their sample. That block reaches the agents as `cancellation.case_policy` on the Evidence Pack.
  71→
  72→## Layout
  73→
  74→```
  75→data/packs/<pack>/
  76→├── disputes/           one JSON file per case, named <dispute_id>.json
  77→├── ground-truth.json   the labels, deliberately kept out of the records
  78→└── pack.json           the manifest: name, format, case count, schema extensions
  79→```
  80→
  81→The labels live in a separate file on purpose. A label inside a dispute record would be visible
  82→to the agents through the intake or trip blocks, and every accuracy number measured against it
  83→would be worthless. `tests/test_corpus.py` enforces this: it scans each record for ground-truth
  84→keys and fails if one leaks.
  85→
  86→## The label shape
  87→
  88→```json
  89→{
  90→  "dispute_id": "RD-0101",
  91→  "category": "route_deviation",
  92→  "expected_outcome": "ruled",
  93→  "expected_action": "refund",
  94→  "expected_amount_sgd": 5.81,
  95→  "decisive_rule_ids": ["RD-1", "RD-2", "RD-3"],
  96→  "rationale": "50% / 3.2 km deviation clears both limbs of RD-1..."
  97→}
  98→```
  99→
 100→`expected_outcome` is one of `ruled`, `escalated`, `human_review`. `decisive_rule_ids` are the
 101→policy rules a correct ruling must rest on — a system that reaches the right answer by citing the
 102→wrong rule got there by luck, and the labels are built so that shows up.
 103→
 104→`rationale` exists so a human reviewer can disagree with a label. An unexplained label cannot be
 105→challenged, which makes it an assertion rather than ground truth.
 106→
 107→## Coverage
 108→
 109→| Cases | | |
 110→|---|---|---|
 111→| Route deviation | 9 | RD-0101 … RD-0109 |
 112→| No-show / cancellation fee | 7 | NS-0201 … NS-0207 |
 113→| Out of scope | 1 | OS-0301 |
 114→
 115→| Outcome | Cases |
 116→|---|---|
 117→| `ruled` → refund | 7 |
 118→| `ruled` → no action | 6 |
 119→| `escalated` | 3 |
 120→| `human_review` | 1 |
 121→
 122→**The balance is deliberate.** Roughly half the ruled cases find for the complainant and half do
 123→not. A corpus where every claim succeeds cannot demonstrate that the system is capable of saying
 124→no, and a dispute resolver that only ever refunds is not adjudicating — it is processing.
 125→`test_corpus.py` asserts both directions are present.
 126→
 127→Three cases escalate rather than resolve, for three different reasons: missing decisive evidence
 128→(RD-0108), an amount above the autonomous cap (RD-0109), and irreconcilable accounts the telemetry
 129→cannot settle (NS-0205). Escalation is a correct outcome under the policy, so it has to be in the
 130→corpus or the escalation path is untested.
 131→
 132→## What each case is for
 133→
 134→**Route deviation**
 135→
 136→| ID | Tests | Expected |
 137→|---|---|---|
 138→| RD-0101 | Plain unjustified detour, both RD-1 limbs cleared | refund 5.81 |
 139→| RD-0102 | Material deviation the rider asked for (added stop) | no action |
 140→| RD-0103 | Deviation below both thresholds — routing judgement, not breach | no action |
 141→| RD-0104 | Long trip where the gross-km limb fires and the percentage barely does | refund 7.70 |
 142→| RD-0105 | Material unjustified deviation, but the rider paid the quoted fixed fare | no action |
 143→| RD-0106 | Fare breakdown does not reconcile — an overcharge with no deviation | refund 3.40 |
 144→| RD-0107 | Big duration overrun, negligible distance variance — traffic, not detour | no action |
 145→| RD-0108 | No estimated distance in the record, so materiality cannot be tested | escalate |
 146→| RD-0109 | Clear-cut deviation whose remedy exceeds the SGD 50 autonomous cap | escalate |
 147→
 148→RD-0109 is load-bearing beyond its label. It is the regression case for ESC-4: an adversarial
 149→review found the cap was stated in this document and in the labels but enforced **nowhere in
 150→code**, and a live run delivered "refund of SGD 55.16" straight to the parties at confidence 0.86.
 151→The cap is now a Python gate in `app/agents/judge.py` alongside the confidence gate, and
 152→`tests/test_gates.py` fails if it ever regresses.
 153→
 154→**No-show / cancellation fee**
 155→
 156→| ID | Tests | Expected |
 157→|---|---|---|
 158→| NS-0201 | Driver at pickup, waited 5.5 min — the fee was earned | no action |
 159→| NS-0202 | Driver at pickup but cancelled after 1.5 min, short of the minimum wait | refund 6.61 |
 160→| NS-0203 | Driver marked arrival 885 m away — the wait never started | refund 6.61 |
 161→| NS-0204 | Driver never arrived at all; rider charged for cancelling | refund 6.61 |
 162→| NS-0205 | Both sides assert opposite facts and no driver position was recorded | escalate |
 163→| NS-0206 | Cancellation inside the 3-minute free window | refund 6.61 |
 164→| NS-0207 | Waiting fee on a completed trip, driver at pickup | no action |
 165→
 166→**Out of scope**
 167→
 168→| ID | Tests | Expected |
 169→|---|---|---|
 170→| OS-0301 | A property-damage claim filed by a driver | human review, no agent ruling |
 171→
 172→RD-0103 carries a second purpose: its rider profile has a high dispute rate and a low trip count.
 173→The claim fails on RD-1's thresholds and **not** on the rider's history, which is what GEN-8
 174→requires. If a system starts declining claims because of who filed them, this is the case where
 175→that shows.
 176→
 177→## How it is generated
 178→
 179→`tools/build_corpus.py` writes both packs — `ryde-synth-v1` itself, and `organiser-style-v1` by
 180→transforming those records through `tools/organiser_pack.py` and copying in the organiser samples
 181→from `tools/organiser_samples/` as received. Both are **non-app tools**: nothing under `app/`
 182→imports from them.
 183→
 184→```bash
 185→python3 tools/build_corpus.py            # regenerate both packs into data/
 186→python3 tools/build_corpus.py --check    # fail if data/ differs from the generator
 187→```
 188→
 189→The generator exists because every case carries fare arithmetic and a GPS polyline that must agree
 190→with each other. Hand-written JSON drifts: a distance edited without recomputing the fare produces
 191→a record where the Evidence Pack calculates something different from what the case intends, and
 192→the label silently becomes a lie. Here the numbers derive from a handful of per-case parameters
 193→(actual km, quoted km, minutes, tariff), so they cannot come apart.
 194→
 195→**GPS traces are generated, not asserted.** Each route is a polyline walked along a bearing in
 196→equal legs, whose haversine length is the intended distance. The Evidence Pack then recomputes the
 197→distance from those points exactly as it would for a real trace — `test_corpus.py` asserts the
 198→pack never fell back to a stated distance. The traces are geometrically valid but they are not
 199→real Singapore roads; they start near Dhoby Ghaut and head northeast in a gentle zigzag.
 200→
 201→**Fares are computed with the pack's own formula**, `(base + per_km × km + per_min × min) × surge
 202→− promo`, and the breakdown components are the same terms with surge applied, so they sum to the
 203→charge. RD-0106 deliberately breaks that reconciliation by 3.40 — it is the only case where the
 204→breakdown is inconsistent, and that inconsistency is the thing being tested.
 205→
 206→## Verification
 207→
 208→`tests/test_corpus.py` (28 tests) is the guard on this artifact. It checks structure (every case
 209→labelled exactly once, no label leaking into a record, every label carrying a rationale), policy
 210→agreement (no label cites a rule that is not in `docs/policy.md`, and the thresholds the tests use
 211→are parsed from the policy's own parameters table rather than trusted as copies), and — the part
 212→that matters most — **evidence agreement**: every labelled refund amount must match a number the
 213→Evidence Pack actually computes from that record, and the policy's mechanical thresholds applied
 214→to the pack must not contradict the label.
 215→
 216→That last check earned its place during authoring. It caught two labels whose amounts were written
 217→by hand and were wrong: RD-0101 was labelled 4.81 against a computed 5.81, and RD-0109 was labelled
 218→below the autonomous cap when its real delta was above it. Both were fixed by correcting the label
 219→and the case, not the test.
 220→
 221→**The guard was then audited by mutation testing**, and it was narrower than it claimed. Six
 222→deliberate corruptions passed a green suite: editing a threshold in the policy's parameters table,
 223→flipping a label's category (which silently disabled every evidence check for that case), flipping
 224→a record's category, putting a non-zero amount on a no-action label, pre-committing an amount on an
 225→escalated label, and raising the runtime cap above the policy's. Each now has a test and each now
 226→fails. The lesson worth keeping: a guard is only as good as the last attempt to defeat it, and the
 227→comment in the test file claiming it caught policy-threshold drift was simply untrue until someone
 228→tried it.
 229→
 230→Every case also runs end to end through the real pipeline without error.
 231→
 232→### Evaluation
 233→
 234→Run `python3 -m app.eval` to evaluate every labelled case. Use `--pack NAME` repeatedly to select
 235→packs, `--llm mock|tencent` to choose the provider, and `--out DIR` to choose the output root.
 236→Reports land under `<out>/<pack>/report.json` and `<out>/<pack>/report.md`, with case artifacts
 237→beside them. “Decisions matching the label” means outcome, action, and cent-rounded amount agree
 238→with the label. “Rulings citing every decisive rule” means every non-`ESC-` decisive label rule
 239→appears in the candidate's citations. Stopping to ask the party counts as a miss. A mock run
 240→checks wiring only; this section makes no score claim.
 241→
 242→## Known limitations
 243→
 244→- **Seventeen cases is a demonstration corpus, not a benchmark.** It is sized to cover every rule
 245→  path and every outcome, not to support a statistically meaningful accuracy claim. Do not quote a
 246→  percentage from it without the denominator attached.
 247→- **No adversarial or ambiguous-language cases.** Every intake form is coherently written. Real
 248→  filings are terse, contradictory, and sometimes in Singlish. A system tuned on this corpus will
 249→  look better than it is on real text.
 250→- **Chat logs are short and clean.** The lexicon signals in the pack fire predictably here, which
 251→  makes them look more informative than GEN-9 says they are.
 252→- **One trip archetype.** All routes are generated from the same bearing-walk, so their geometry is
 253→  more uniform than a real fleet's.
 254→- **The labels are ours.** Where the policy is `[SYNTHESISED]`, the "correct" answer is a judgement
 255→  the team made. A Ryde operations reviewer might rule differently on RD-0104 or RD-0105, and that
 256→  disagreement would be about policy, not about the system.
 257→
 258→## If a real dataset arrives
 259→
 260→Drop it in as a new pack — `data/packs/<name>/` with `disputes/`, `ground-truth.json` and
 261→`pack.json` — in either record shape (both are documented at the top of `app/dispute.py`), then set
 262→`dataset_pack` in `app/config.json` or pass `--pack <name>`. Keep this corpus as the **held-out
 263→labelled set**: a real dataset supplied without ground-truth labels cannot measure accuracy, so the
 264→synthesised labelled corpus stays useful even when it is no longer the primary input.
 265→

1→# Ryde — Multi-Agent Autonomous Dispute Resolution
   2→
   3→Entry for the **Tencent Cloud "AI CAN DO IT" Hackathon Singapore 2026**, Digital Native track
   4→(the Ryde challenge statement, section 5 of the organisers' document).
   5→
   6→**Status: building (since 2026-09-21).** The scope
   7→is ruled: a two-category MVP (route deviation + no-show charge) with three agents, a
   8→deterministic evidence layer, and an observable case-file view. The challenge statement is in
   9→[`docs/statement-extract.md`](docs/statement-extract.md); the builder's contract is in
  10→[`CODEBUDDY.md`](CODEBUDDY.md).
  11→
  12→## The challenge
  13→
  14→Ride-hailing platforms process thousands of dispute tickets daily: fare disputes, route deviations,
  15→property damage, safety incidents, no-show charges. They are subjective, emotionally charged, and
  16→currently resolved by humans reviewing GPS telemetry, chat logs, payment records and company policy
  17→by hand. The result is slow, expensive and inconsistent.
  18→
  19→The task is an autonomous multi-agent system that gathers evidence, builds both sides' cases, applies
  20→company policy and issues a fair ruling with a confidence score and a plain-language explanation.
  21→
  22→## Architecture
  23→
  24→Three core agents, all MVP-required:
  25→
  26→| Agent | Role |
  27→|---|---|
  28→| **Rider Advocate** | Builds the rider's case from the Evidence Pack and the policy |
  29→| **Driver Advocate** | Builds the driver's case from the Evidence Pack and the policy |
  30→| **Judge** | Weighs both cases, applies policy, rules, and explains the reasoning with a confidence score |
  31→
  32→Inter-agent communication must be **observable** — a judge needs to see how the agents exchange
  33→information and build their cases. That surface is a required deliverable, not a nice-to-have.
  34→
  35→The full walkthrough — components, lifecycle, gates, observability — is in
  36→[`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md). The system on one page:
  37→
  38→```mermaid
  39→flowchart TD
  40→    PACK["Dataset pack"] --> B["Server"]
  41→    PACK --> CL["Command-line runner"]
  42→    A["Rider intake form"] --> B
  43→    B --> C{"Category in scope?"}
  44→    CL --> C
  45→    C -- "Out of scope" --> H["Human review"]
  46→    C -- "Route deviation or no-show" --> E["Evidence Pack"]
  47→    POL["Policy document"] --> RA["Rider Advocate"]
  48→    POL --> DA["Driver Advocate"]
  49→    POL --> J["Judge"]
  50→    E --> RA
  51→    E --> DA
  52→    RA --> S{"Questions for the party?"}
  53→    DA --> S
  54→    S -- "Yes, first round" --> O4["Needs info"]
  55→    O4 --> PA["Party answers follow-ups"]
  56→    PA -- "Fresh run with the answers" --> B
  57→    S -- "No" --> J
  58→    J --> G{"Gates pass? Confidence, cap, measured deviation"}
  59→    G -- "Yes" --> O1["Ruled"]
  60→    G -- "No" --> O2["Withheld"]
  61→    O2 -- "Candidate ruling queued" --> H
  62→    B -. "Every step emits an event" .-> L["Event log"]
  63→    J -.-> L
  64→    L -- "Embedded in the case file" --> K["Operator console"]
  65→```

  75→
  76→## Development tooling
  77→
  78→Built with Tencent Cloud **CodeBuddy**. The competition mandates proof of product usage, so
  79→development happens in the tool and evidence is captured as it occurs.
  80→
  81→## Run
  82→
  83→No dependencies and no API key needed for the skeleton: it runs on a stock Python 3.9+ with the
  84→standard library only, using a deterministic mock in place of the LLM.
  85→
  86→```bash
  87→python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
  88→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0101
  89→python3 -m app.cli --pack organiser-style-v1 --dispute DISP-002
  90→```
  91→
  92→`--dispute` takes either a dispute id inside the selected pack or a path to a record file
  93→(`python3 -m app.cli --dispute data/packs/ryde-synth-v1/disputes/RD-0101.json`). The pack
  94→defaults to `dataset_pack` in `app/config.json`; `--pack` overrides it for one run.
  95→
  96→That prints the agent-to-agent event strip and the ruling, and writes the run's artifacts to
  97→`runs/<run_id>/`: `events.jsonl` (the observable traffic), `payloads/*.json` (the full payload
  98→behind each event) and `case_file.json` (evidence, both claims, resolution).
  99→
 100→The corpus lives in two swappable packs under `data/packs/`: `ryde-synth-v1` (our 17 labelled
 101→cases, our record shape) and `organiser-style-v1` (the same 17 cases as twins in the organisers'
 102→shape, plus the organisers' own `DISP-002` verbatim). `RD-0103` is a deviation too small to
 103→matter, `NS-0203` is a driver who marked arrival 885 m from the pickup point, `RD-0109` is a
 104→remedy above the autonomous cap that the system refuses to issue on its own, and `OS-0301` is an
 105→out-of-scope filing routed to human review without an LLM call. `docs/dataset.md` maps each case
 106→to what it tests; `<pack>/ground-truth.json` holds the expected outcomes, deliberately kept out
 107→of the records the agents see.
 108→
 109→Three gates stand between a ruling and the parties, and **all three are enforced in Python, not
 110→asked of the model in a prompt**: the confidence threshold, ESC-4's SGD 50 autonomous cap, and
 111→ESC-2, which withholds a route-case ruling when the deviation cannot be measured. Try them:
 112→
 113→```bash
 114→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0109   # withheld: above the cap
 115→python3 -m app.cli --pack ryde-synth-v1 --dispute RD-0108   # withheld: no deviation to measure
 116→```
 117→
 118→**Mock by default.** The default provider is a deterministic mock. Its free-text fields (claim
 119→summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation) are prefixed `MOCK`; actions, amounts, rule IDs and
 120→evidence refs are not. A mock run is a plumbing demonstration, never a real ruling. The real model is
 121→Tencent Cloud ADP, one app per agent: put the three app keys in `.env` (see `.env.example`), then
 122→run `python3 -m app.server --llm tencent` or `python3 -m app.cli --llm tencent --dispute <id>`.
 123→

 111→def _ruling_proves_real_provider(resolution: Dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
 112→    """True only when the resolution's ruling carries a proven real-provider LLM record.
 113→
 114→    A shape check, not a type check: the record must be a non-array dict (which in
 115→    Python excludes lists) and its "provider" value must be exactly REAL_PROVIDER —
 116→    a list or object inside the field, or a near-miss string, does not count.
 117→    """
 118→    ruling = resolution.get("ruling")
 119→    if not isinstance(ruling, dict):
 120→        return False
 121→    llm = ruling.get("llm")
 122→    if not isinstance(llm, dict):
 123→        return False
 124→    return llm.get("provider") == REAL_PROVIDER

 763→class _ServerState:
 764→    """Everything one server instance needs to run a dispute."""
 765→
 766→    def __init__(self, pack_dir: Path, out_dir: Path, llm: LLMClient, confidence_threshold: float,
 767→                 autonomous_cap_sgd: float, policy):
 768→        self.pack_dir = pack_dir
 769→        self.out_dir = out_dir
 770→        self.llm = llm
 771→        self.confidence_threshold = confidence_threshold
 772→        self.autonomous_cap_sgd = autonomous_cap_sgd
 773→        self.policy = policy
 774→
 775→
 776→def make_server(
 777→    port: int,
 778→    pack_dir: Optional[Path] = None,
 779→    out_dir: Optional[Path] = None,
 780→    llm: Optional[LLMClient] = None,
 781→    provider: Optional[str] = None,
 782→) -> ThreadingHTTPServer:
 783→    """An HTTP server bound to 127.0.0.1 only.
 784→
 785→    `None` means the app/config.json default for that setting; `llm=None` builds the
 786→    provider named by `provider`, or the configured one when that is None too. A real
 787→    provider is built here, at startup, so missing keys stop the server before any
 788→    party files a dispute. Tests pass port=0 and read the bound port back.
 789→    """
 790→    config = load_config()
 791→    resolved_pack = Path(pack_dir) if pack_dir is not None else config.dataset_pack_dir
 792→    resolved_out = Path(out_dir) if out_dir is not None else config.out_dir
 793→    if llm is None:
 794→        provider = provider or config.llm.provider
 795→        if provider == "tencent":
 796→            llm = build_llm_client(provider, settings=config.llm)
 797→        else:
 798→            llm = build_llm_client(provider)
 799→    policy = load_policy(config.policy_path)
 800→
 801→    httpd = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), RydeRequestHandler)
 802→    httpd.ryde_state = _ServerState(  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
 803→        pack_dir=resolved_pack,
 804→        out_dir=resolved_out,
 805→        llm=llm,
 806→        confidence_threshold=config.confidence_threshold,
 807→        autonomous_cap_sgd=config.autonomous_cap_sgd,
 808→        policy=policy,
 809→    )
 810→    return httpd
 811→
 812→
 813→def parse_args(argv: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> argparse.Namespace:
 814→    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
 815→        prog="python3 -m app.server",
 816→        description="Serve the party page and the operator console on 127.0.0.1.",
 817→    )
 818→    parser.add_argument(
 819→        "--llm",
 820→        choices=["mock", "tencent"],
 821→        default=None,
 822→        help="LLM provider (default: app/config.json). 'tencent' calls the three ADP apps "
 823→        "and needs their keys in .env.",
 824→    )
 825→    return parser.parse_args(argv)
 826→
 827→
 828→def main(argv: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> int:
 829→    args = parse_args(argv)
 830→    httpd = make_server(DEFAULT_PORT, provider=args.llm)
 831→    port = httpd.server_address[1]
 832→    print("Ryde party surface on http://127.0.0.1:%d" % port)
 833→    print("  party page:   http://127.0.0.1:%d/party/" % port)
 834→    print("  console:      http://127.0.0.1:%d/" % port)
 835→    print("  llm provider: %s" % httpd.ryde_state.llm.provider_name)  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
 836→    try:
 837→        httpd.serve_forever()
 838→    except KeyboardInterrupt:
 839→        pass
 840→    finally:
 841→        httpd.server_close()
 842→    return 0
 843→
 844→
 845→if __name__ == "__main__":
 846→    sys.exit(main())

def _ask(self, *, system_prompt, user_prompt, metadata=None, build):
    attempts = transient_used = reasks_used = 0
    while True:
        remaining = self._budget.remaining()
        if remaining is not None and remaining < MIN_CALL_SECONDS:
            raise ModelFailure(kind="time budget", attempts=attempts, ...) from None
        attempts += 1
        request = LLMRequest(agent=self.name, ..., timeout_seconds=remaining)
        try:
            response = self.llm.complete(request)
            payload = parse_json_object(response.text, agent=self.name)
            provenance = response.as_log_fields()
            provenance["request_fingerprint"] = request.fingerprint()
            return build(payload, provenance)          # <-- ContractError raised here
        except (LLMContractError, ContractError) as exc:
            if reasks_used >= self._budget.contract_reasks:
                raise ModelFailure(kind="unreadable reply", attempts=attempts, message=str(exc)) from None
            reasks_used += 1
            self._emit_retry(attempt=attempts, kind="unreadable reply", message=str(exc), wait=0.0)
        except LLMTransientError as exc:
            if transient_used >= len(self._budget.delays_seconds):
                raise ModelFailure(kind="transient", attempts=attempts, message=str(exc)) from None
            delay = self._budget.delays_seconds[transient_used]
            remaining = self._budget.remaining()
            if remaining is not None and remaining < delay + MIN_CALL_SECONDS:
                raise ModelFailure(kind="time budget", attempts=attempts, message=str(exc)) from None
            transient_used += 1
            self._emit_retry(attempt=attempts, kind="transient", message=str(exc), wait=delay)
            self._sleep(delay)
        except LLMError as exc:
            raise ModelFailure(kind="permanent", attempts=attempts, message=str(exc)) from None

## Pitfalls and Python 3.9 concerns

**Exception taxonomy**
1. `LLMContractError` and `LLMTransientError` are siblings under `LLMError`; a broad `except LLMError` written before them silently reclassifies everything as permanent. Order the clauses specific → general, and put `ContractError` (a `ValueError`, **not** an `LLMError`) in the same clause as `LLMContractError`.
2. `urllib.error.HTTPError` is a subclass of `URLError`, which is an `OSError`; the HTTPError clause must stay first in `_post` or 4xx/5xx stop being classified. `http.client.HTTPException` is *not* an `OSError`, so it needs its own clause before the `OSError` one.
3. The firewall check must precede the 429/5xx transient rule (a 503 carrying `waf-captcha` is permanent), and `_parse_events` must keep its marker check for a 200 that is really a captcha page.
4. `type(exc)(message)` only works because every current error takes one string. Keep it in `complete()` only; the adapter's own raises construct the intended class directly.

**Retry/budget semantics**
5. Attempts are **per agent**, counted when a call is about to start. A budget refusal before the first call must report `attempts=0` (the judge in the 93 s test); a refusal before a *retry* reports the attempts already made (1 in the 60 s test).
6. The two refusals are different checks: before a call `remaining < 5.0`; before a wait `remaining < delay + 5.0`, and the wait check must happen **before** sleeping (the test asserts `clock.slept == []`). Getting `<` vs `<=` wrong is a one-test flip.
7. Compute `remaining` (and therefore `timeout_seconds`) at the **top** of the loop, before `llm.complete`, or the 120/110/100 sequence drifts by one call cost.
8. `run_dispute(retry_policy=None)` must default to a real `RetryPolicy()` (real clock/sleep, unlimited budget), not "no retry": `test_pipeline.ContractFailureTest` and `StringAmountRulingTest` rely on the re-ask happening (2 calls, `attempts=2`). The only test that lets the default policy sleep patches `time.sleep`; every other scripted failure in the suite is a plain `LLMError` (permanent) or the mock (never fails), so no real 2/5/10 s waits occur.
9. The contract re-ask and the transient retry counters are independent; a re-ask must not consume a transient retry (pinned by `test_the_two_counters_are_separate`).
10. Only the failing agent is re-called — do not put the loop around a whole advocate/judge pair.
11. `time.sleep`/`time.monotonic` must be resolved at call time (`(self._budget.sleep or time.sleep)(...)`, `(self.clock or time.monotonic)()`), never bound at import or construction, or `mock.patch("time.sleep")` misses.

**Escalation/pipeline**
12. Catch `ModelFailure` only around the three agent calls. A wider `try` would swallow a `TypeError`/`KeyError` from the evidence layer or the builder, breaking ruling 3.
13. Escalation must **return normally** — that is what keeps `dispute.json` written, the round-two claim held (409 on replay) and the server's `rmtree` from firing.
14. `Resolution.to_dict()` must always include `model_failure` (even `None`); `party_view` must not be touched, and its five-key allowlist must stay clean of `firewall`/`501`/`model`/`judge`/`attempt`/`error`.
15. Keep `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`, `FIREWALL_FIXTURE` handling and the private test-helper signatures (`_Transport`, `_SizedResponse`, `_patched`, `_client`, `_request`) exactly as they are — `test_w19` imports them from the ADP test modules.

**Python 3.9**
16. No `match`, no `X | Y` unions, no `tuple[...]`/`list[...]` in runtime-evaluated positions: use `Optional[...]`, `Tuple[...]`, `Callable[...]`, `Dict[...]`, `List[...]`.
17. Frozen dataclasses with a tuple default are fine; do not use `field(default_factory=...)` for the delays.
18. `dataclasses.replace(real.llm, case_budget_seconds=...)` in the tests requires `LLMSettings` to be a dataclass field — give it a default (`120.0`) so no other construction site breaks.

**Docs traps**
19. `test_architecture_doc.test_names_every_event_type` will fail until architecture.md names **both** new event types with backticks — this is not optional cleanup.
20. The W19 doc test bans the literal `generic error` anywhere in architecture.md and the regex `Any failure raises an\s+error`; both live in text being rewritten, so delete, don't paraphrase.

**Behavioural details that are easy to miss**

   2→
   3→Every agent gets the same material (the dispute intake, the Evidence Pack, the policy

   5→contract. The differences between agents are their role text and their output schema.
   6→
   7→The hard rules are the ones the locked scope demands: no arithmetic by an agent (every
   8→number comes from the pack), evidence cited by dotted field reference, policy cited by
   9→rule ID, and nothing invented. Citations are validated against the pack and the policy
  10→document after every call; anything that does not resolve is recorded on the case rather
  11→than quietly dropped, so the case file shows what the model actually claimed.

 175→) -> Dict[str, Any]:
 176→    """Check every citation against the pack and the policy document.

 178→    Nothing is removed: the case keeps the model's own claims, and the failures are
 179→    recorded alongside them so the case file shows what was claimed and what resolved.
 180→    """

 182→    unknown_refs = [ref for ref in cited_refs if ref not in legal_refs]
 183→    unknown_rules = policy.unknown_rule_ids(cited_rules)

def _escalated_on_model_failure(
    *,
    dispute: Dispute,
    events: EventLog,
    policy: PolicySet,
    pack: Any,
    threshold: float,
    rider_case: Optional[AdvocateCase],
    driver_case: Optional[AdvocateCase],
    failure: ModelFailure,
    extra_notes: Optional[List[str]] = None,
) -> CaseFile:
    """Keep the work done so far and queue a failed model call for human review."""
    notes = [
        "the model could not answer for %s: %s after %d attempt(s)"
        % (failure.agent, failure.kind, failure.attempts)
    ] + list(extra_notes or [])
    resolution = Resolution(
        dispute_id=dispute.dispute_id,
        outcome="withheld",
        party_message=UNDER_REVIEW_MESSAGE,
        confidence_threshold=threshold,
        ruling=None,
        withheld_candidate=None,
        escalated_for_human_review=True,
        notes=notes,
        model_failure=failure.to_dict(),
    )
    events.emit(
        EventType.DISPUTE_ESCALATED_ON_MODEL_FAILURE,
        from_=Actor.SYSTEM,
        to=Actor.HUMAN_REVIEW,
        summary="model failure in %s: %s after %d attempt(s)"
        % (failure.agent, failure.kind, failure.attempts),
        payload={
            "dispute_id": dispute.dispute_id,
            "failure": failure.to_dict(),
        },
    )
    events.emit(
        EventType.PARTY_NOTIFIED,
        from_=Actor.SYSTEM,
        to=Actor.PARTIES,
        summary="parties notified: your case is still under review",
        payload={
            "dispute_id": dispute.dispute_id,
            "outcome": resolution.outcome,
            "message": resolution.party_message,
        },
    )
    case_file = CaseFile(
        run_id=events.run_id,
        dispute_id=dispute.dispute_id,
        category=dispute.category,
        generated_at=_now(),
        confidence_threshold=threshold,
        policy_path=_policy_source_path(policy),
        policy_rule_ids=policy.rule_ids(),
        intake=_intake_section(dispute),

        rider_case=rider_case.to_dict() if rider_case is not None else None,
        driver_case=driver_case.to_dict() if driver_case is not None else None,
        resolution=resolution.to_dict(),
    )
    _complete(events, case_file, resolution)

 334→    nothing survives, the run does not stop (an empty needs_info is worse than none).
 335→    """
 336→    if dispute.filed_by == "rider":
 337→        collected = list(rider_case.follow_up_questions) + list(driver_case.follow_up_questions)
 338→    else:
 339→        collected = list(driver_case.follow_up_questions) + list(rider_case.follow_up_questions)
 340→
 341→    gated: List[str] = []
 342→    seen: set = set()
 343→    for question in collected:
 344→        if len(gated) >= 3:
 345→            break
 346→        text = (question or "").strip()
 347→        if not text or not is_party_safe(text):
 348→            continue
 349→        key = _normalised_question(text)
 350→        if not key or key in seen:
 351→            continue
 352→        seen.add(key)
 353→        gated.append(text)
 354→
 355→    if gated:
 356→        return gated
 357→
 358→    # Fallback: nothing the advocates wrote is safe to send. Ask about the blank
 359→    # intake fields in code-built words, one per field, in form order — the label
 360→    # table is the one owner of those words.
 361→    labels = dict(INTAKE_QUESTIONS.get(dispute.category, ()))
 362→    return [
 363→        blank_field_question(labels[key])
 364→        for key in labels
 365→        if isinstance(dispute.intake.get(key), str) and not dispute.intake[key].strip()
 366→    ][:3]

 217→the dispute record, the evidence pack and the policy — never the answer — so replayed-run
 218→consistency can be measured honestly.
 219→
 220→## LLM provider
 221→
 222→Agent logic never talks to a vendor SDK. Every agent builds a request and calls one seam:
 223→the `LLMClient` interface in `app/llm/`, a single `complete` method whose response carries
 224→the text plus provenance (provider, model, usage, finish reason). Two adapters implement
 225→it. The mock provider, `app/llm/mock.py`, returns deterministic contract-shaped responses,
 226→so the full pipeline runs with no API key and the same dispute always produces the same
 227→decisions and the same computed figures (the run id and the event timestamps differ from
 228→run to run). Its free-text fields — claim summaries, arguments, the Judge's explanation —
 229→carry a `MOCK` prefix, so a mock run can never be mistaken for a real ruling; actions, rule
 230→IDs and evidence refs are not prefixed. The party decision message, composed in code, is
 231→marked differently: on a decided party view it leads with a fixed demo notice stating that
 232→the decision came from an illustrative run and is not a live review, shown whenever the
 233→ruling's LLM record does not prove the Tencent provider, and only a record whose provider
 234→field is exactly `tencent` shows a decision with no notice. The Tencent adapter,
 235→`app/llm/tencent.py`, implements the same interface over Tencent Cloud ADP (Agent
 236→Development Platform). Each agent is its own published ADP app with its own key: Rider
 237→Advocate, Driver Advocate and Judge. The apps carry only a short role card; the adapter
 238→sends the full role prompt on every call, so the prompts live in this repo and every gate
 239→stays in Python. Three things about the endpoint shape the adapter. Tencent's web firewall
 240→blocks prompts that mix backticks with ASCII brackets, so the adapter drops backticks and
 241→sends full-width brackets, which the model reads the same way; a blocked call raises an
 242→error and is never retried. ADP reports errors inside a successful HTTP response, so the
 243→adapter reads every event rather than trusting the status code. The free plan allows 10
 244→calls a minute, so calls are spaced at least 6.5 seconds apart. Any failure raises an
 245→error, and there is no silent fallback to the mock. The mock stays the default provider,
 246→so the tests and a fresh checkout need no keys; `--llm tencent` selects the real model.
 247→
 248→## Limits
 249→
 250→What the system does not do yet, stated plainly:
 251→
 252→- **A failed model call is an error, not a referral.** If a live call fails (the firewall,
 253→  the rate limit, an ADP error or a reply that breaks the output contract), the run stops
 254→  and the party sees a generic error. It is not yet routed to a human reviewer.
 255→- **Amounts must come back as JSON numbers.** A model reply carrying an amount as a string
 256→  is rejected, never converted, because the value moves money.
 257→- **Two categories only.** Route deviation and no-show charge. Property damage and safety
 258→  incidents route to human review by design.
 259→- **The driver-side form is not built.** The party page files as the rider only; the
 260→  pipeline itself accepts driver-filed disputes, but no web form offers it yet.
 261→- **Follow-up wording is code-owned.** Advocates select slot IDs; code renders each question
 262→  from the fixed category bank or an intake form label, and model-written question text is
 263→  ignored. Bank slots are rider-only; form slots are available to either filer.
 264→- **The word check is a backstop.** Rendered follow-up questions and the code-composed decision
 265→  message pass the keyword gate, which is not a semantic guarantee; blank fields still use
 266→  template questions built from the form's own labels.
 267→- **Policy preconditions are not evaluated by code.** The rules are written against pack
 268→  fields in plain language; nothing checks them mechanically, and the Judge applies them by
 269→  reading them.
 270→

## Workflow
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** below.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (example below)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule above.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'Explore', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, cpu cores - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:\${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: \${f.title}`, {label: `verify:\${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`\${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`\${bugs.length} found, \${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "\${b.desc}" via the \${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: \${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.
